query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified, Co‐free FeNiCrMn produced by rapid solidification, the dynamic mechanical response is governed by a dual mechanism in which a high density of dislocations and in situ–formed nanometer‐scale Mn-rich oxide precipitates synergistically control the deformation behavior—providing strong Orowan‐ and dislocation forest–type strengthening at low temperatures and slow strain rates, while at elevated temperatures and higher strain rates enhanced dislocation mobility and partial dynamic recovery steer the response toward lower yield strength with higher ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Rapidly solidified, Co-free FeNiCrMn with a fine-grained microstructure, high dislocation density, and uniformly distributed nano-sized Mn-rich oxide precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the material to uniaxial tensile and/or compressive dynamic tests across a controlled temperature range (from room temperature up to ~900 °C) and varying strain rates.
generation.conditions: Testing in a controlled furnace/environment and strain rate apparatus ensuring constant strain rate and homogenous temperature distribution during deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometer-scale Mn-rich oxide precipitates and a high dislocation network formed during rapid solidification.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures or slower strain rates, the precipitates impede dislocation motion via Orowan looping and contribute to a high dislocation density that increases yield strength and strain hardening. In contrast, at elevated temperatures and higher strain rates, increased dislocation mobility and partial dynamic recovery (or recrystallization) reduce the strengthening effect, thereby shifting the deformation mechanism toward more ductile response.
generation.predicted_outcome: The material should exhibit a marked transition: high yield strength and work hardening with lower ductility at low temperatures/strain rates, transitioning to reduced yield strength but improved ductility at higher temperatures/strain rates. In situ or post-deformation microstructural examination should reveal pronounced interactions between dislocations and the precipitates under low-temperature conditions, with signs of dynamic recovery or partial recrystallization at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: The baseline behavior of as-solidified FeNiCrMn (with high dislocation density and fine precipitates) without additional thermal treatments, showing high strength and moderate ductility under quasi-static conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to samples processed under rapid solidification conditions and tested within a temperature range of ~25 °C to 900 °C and moderate strain rates; conditions outside these ranges (e.g., ultra-high strain rates or post-annealed/coarsened microstructures) may involve additional mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the exact quantitative contribution of the nano-precipitates relative to dislocation density in controlling the dynamic response, and whether the oxide precipitate chemistry in the Co-free system exactly parallels that in comparable Co-containing alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare rapid-solidified FeNiCrMn samples and perform a series of uniaxial tensile and compressive tests across temperatures from 25 °C to 900 °C at several controlled strain rates. Conduct complementary in situ or post-mortem transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterization to assess dislocation structures and precipitate morphology before and after deformation.
measurements: Stress–strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile/compressive strength, ductility)
TEM images quantifying dislocation density and precipitate size/distribution
Microstructural evolution (e.g., evidence of dynamic recovery or recrystallization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental data do not reveal a transition in dynamic behavior (e.g., a shift from Orowan-controlled strengthening at low temperatures to reduced strength with increased ductility at high temperatures) and if TEM does not document the predicted strong dislocation–precipitate interactions or the expected changes in microstructure, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using pre-alloyed spherical powder (average diameter 27.2 µm); laser power 90 W, scan speed 600 mm/s, hatch space 80 µm, layer thickness 25 µm, volumetric energy density 75 J/mm³, 180° rotation scanning pattern, high-purity Ar atmosphere.. Test conditions: Compression tests at 25, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C; initial strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; engineering strain limit 0.4; specimens preheated at 10 °C/min; MoS₂ lubricant used.. Question: What are the creep deformation mechanisms and microstructural evolution characteristics of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy in the intermediate temperature range of 500–600 °C?. System: Equiatomic Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Mn20 (atomic percentage) FCC-structured high-entropy alloy. Processing: Vacuum induction melting with 99.9 mass% purity elements, re-melted five times, drop-cast, homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h, cold-rolled 40%, and annealed at 900 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Tensile creep tests at 500, 550, and 600 °C under applied stresses of 140–400 MPa; interrupted tests at steady-state stages cooled with liquid nitrogen.
